title: Research Practice Throughput Score
subtitle: A 17-question diagnostic for founders, research directors, and COOs running boutique qual/quant practices (10-40 staff). Find which of six handoffs is silently eating 12+ hours per study.

persona_selector.text: Which best describes your role on studies?

answers.label: Owner / Founder / Managing Partner
Research Director / Ops Lead / Project Director
Senior Researcher / Analyst / IC

questions.text: When a new study lands, where does the brief live?

answers.label: Verbal call notes only or scattered email threads
One Google Doc per study, free-form
A standard intake template, mostly filled
A structured intake form (Typeform, Fillout, or equivalent) feeding a project record
Structured intake auto-creates the project space, folders, and kickoff doc

questions.text: How often does a study scope change after kickoff because of an ambiguous brief?

answers.label: Almost every study
Most studies
Roughly half
Occasionally
Rare, under 10% of studies

questions.text: How long does it take you to write a discussion guide or screener from a fresh brief?

answers.label: 6+ hours
3 to 6 hours
2 to 3 hours
60 to 90 minutes
Under 60 minutes, mostly assembled from prior assets

low.headline: Your studies start in the dark
low.text: You are absorbing brief ambiguity as researcher hours later in the study. Every hour saved here compounds because a clean brief prevents fielding rework, transcript confusion, and synthesis dead ends.
steps: Build one structured intake form (Typeform or Fillout) with 12 to 15 required fields covering objectives, audience, deliverable format, and decision the client will make with the findings
Refuse to start any study without the intake completed and signed off, even for repeat clients
Create a template library of 5 to 8 reusable discussion guide and screener modules tagged by study type so the next guide is assembly, not authorship

mid.headline: Intake works, but assembly is still manual
mid.text: Your briefs are usable but the path from brief to discussion guide is still mostly hand-authored. That is where 3 to 6 hours per study quietly disappears.
steps: Connect your intake form to an automation that pre-populates a project doc and a starter discussion guide using prior study assets
Add a 30-minute scope confirmation call with the client between intake and kickoff to catch the 20% of briefs that look clean but are not
Tag every past discussion guide by methodology and audience so a junior researcher can pull a 70% draft in under 20 minutes

high.headline: Intake is a real asset, now protect it
high.text: You have a structured front door. The risk now is drift as the team grows or as one-off client requests bend the template. Treat intake as a product you maintain.
steps: Review your intake form every quarter and prune fields that nobody uses or that produce noisy answers
Add a brief quality score (1 to 5) applied by the PM at kickoff so you can correlate brief quality with downstream rework hours
Pilot AI-assisted guide generation that drafts the discussion guide directly from the intake record, with the researcher editing rather than authoring

questions.text: How are screener results reviewed and approved?

answers.label: Manual eyeball-check on a spreadsheet
Spreadsheet with conditional formatting or filters
Recruiter pre-screens, PM approves manually
Auto-flagging on red flags, human review on the rest
Auto-approval with audit trail, human review only on edge cases

questions.text: How are respondent interviews scheduled and confirmed?

answers.label: Email back-and-forth, manually tracked
Calendly or similar, but reminders are manual
Scheduling tool with automated confirmation emails
Scheduling tool plus automated reminder sequence and reschedule flow
Fully automated invite, reminder, incentive, and no-show recovery pipeline

questions.text: Mid-study, how quickly can you see fielding status (completes, drop-offs, demographic gaps)?

answers.label: Ask the recruiter, wait for a manual update
Recruiter sends a daily email summary
Shared spreadsheet updated once or twice a day
Live dashboard, refreshed but checked manually
Live dashboard with auto-alerts when a quota or pace target slips

questions.text: What is your current no-show or reschedule rate on scheduled interviews?

answers.label: Above 25%
Under 5%

low.headline: Fielding is consuming your senior hours
low.text: Manual screener review and email-based scheduling are a tax paid in PM and director time. This is the single fastest category to fix because the tooling is mature and cheap.
steps: Move screener intake to a tool that supports conditional logic and auto-flagging (Sago, Respondent, or even Typeform with logic) so red flags surface before a human looks
Standardize a 3-touch reminder sequence (24h, 2h, 15min) on every scheduled interview to cut no-show rates in half within one study cycle
Set a daily 5-minute fielding standup with a single shared dashboard view, not a meeting plus a spreadsheet plus a Slack thread

mid.headline: Fielding works, but visibility lags reality
mid.text: Your scheduling and screening are functional. The leak now is that decisions about pace, quotas, and recruiter pressure are made on stale data instead of live signal.
steps: Build a single fielding dashboard (Looker Studio, Metabase, or even a polished Sheet) that updates at least hourly and is the only source of truth
Add automated quota and pace alerts that ping the PM in Slack when a demographic cell falls behind by more than 20%
Run a no-show audit on your last 10 studies to find the 1 or 2 segments driving most of your reschedule load, then add an extra incentive or earlier confirmation for just those segments

high.headline: Fielding is a competitive advantage, now monetize it
high.text: You have the rare combination of automated screening, fast visibility, and low no-show rates. The opportunity is to turn that operational lead into pricing power or faster turnaround as a sold deliverable.
steps: Package a 'fielding in 5 business days' SLA into your proposals and price it as a premium tier
Document your fielding playbook so a new project director can run it without you in the loop, freeing your senior time for synthesis and client work
Measure recruiter-by-recruiter performance on completion rate and time-to-first-complete and consolidate spend on the top 2 or 3

answers.label: Manual transcription by a staff member or vendor, multi-day turnaround
Generic transcription service, edited by hand
AI transcription (Otter, Descript, or similar), reviewed manually
AI transcription with automated speaker labels and timestamps, light review
AI transcription plus automated cleanup, redaction, and PII handling, minimal review

questions.text: How are interview files, transcripts, and notes named and organized?

answers.label: Whatever the researcher chose, scattered across drives
Per-study folder, inconsistent file names
Per-study folder with a documented naming convention, mostly followed
Per-study folder with enforced naming and an index file
Automated naming and folder creation from the intake record, no manual filing

questions.text: How long after an interview is the transcript ready for the analyst to work with?

answers.label: 3+ days
1 to 2 days
Same day, late
Within 2 to 4 hours
Within 30 minutes, automated

low.headline: Transcripts are a hidden bottleneck
low.text: Slow or messy transcripts push synthesis into a panic at the end of the study and force analysts to work from memory instead of evidence. This is cheap to fix and has an immediate compounding effect on report quality.
steps: Adopt one AI transcription tool (Otter, Descript, or Fireflies) across the whole practice this month, no per-project exceptions
Write a one-page file naming and folder convention and enforce it with a checklist at the end of every fielding day
Move transcript generation to within 4 hours of the interview so the analyst can start coding while context is fresh

mid.headline: Transcripts are usable, prep is still slow
mid.text: You have decent tooling but the path from raw recording to analyst-ready transcript still has manual steps. Those steps are where junior time leaks.
steps: Automate the post-transcription cleanup (speaker labels, filler word removal, PII redaction) with a script or an n8n flow rather than manual editing
Index every transcript with consistent metadata (study ID, respondent segment, date) so cross-study lookups become possible later
Audit your last 5 studies for how many hours went into file management versus actual analysis, the gap is your fix target

high.headline: Your data is analysis-ready by default
high.text: You have one of the rare practices where transcripts are not the bottleneck. The next move is to turn that clean data into a long-term asset.
steps: Start tagging transcripts with structured metadata so you can pull cross-study insights for thought leadership or repeat-client trend reports
Pilot a private RAG setup over your transcript library so analysts can query past studies in seconds instead of digging
Sell historical pattern reports to repeat clients as a paid add-on, your clean data makes it possible where competitors cannot

answers.label: Highlighter and memory, no codebook
Codebook in a doc, manual tagging in transcripts
Dedicated tool (Dovetail, Reduct, NVivo) used inconsistently
Dedicated tool used on every study with a maintained codebook
AI-assisted coding with human review and a versioned shared codebook

questions.text: How do themes get from coded data to a defensible finding?

answers.label: Lead researcher writes it from memory
Affinity mapping in a workshop, output captured in slides
Affinity mapping plus quote pulls, manually compiled
Structured synthesis template populated from the coding tool
Synthesis template auto-populated with quotes and counts, researcher curates and interprets

questions.text: How fast can a researcher find every quote on a specific theme across a study?

answers.label: Hours of re-reading
30 to 60 minutes with Ctrl+F across transcripts
15 to 30 minutes using a coding tool
Under 10 minutes via tag search
Seconds via search across a tagged library

questions.text: If two researchers coded the same 5 transcripts, how similar would their themes be?

answers.label: Very different, no shared frame
Same broad themes, different labels
Mostly aligned with a shared codebook
Strongly aligned, minor variance
Near identical, codebook governance is mature

low.headline: Synthesis depends on one person remembering
low.text: This is the highest-risk category because it concentrates knowledge in individuals and makes findings hard to defend to a skeptical client. It also caps how many studies your senior people can ship per quarter.
steps: Build a single codebook this quarter, even a rough one, and require every study to apply it before any synthesis work begins
Pick one coding tool (Dovetail or Reduct are the easiest entry points) and standardize on it for every study within 60 days
Run a 2-researcher calibration exercise on the next study where both code the same 3 transcripts and reconcile differences, this is the fastest way to lift consistency

mid.headline: Coding is consistent, synthesis is still slow
mid.text: You have a codebook and a tool but the leap from coded data to a written finding still takes a senior person too long. AI assistance is finally good enough to compress this.
steps: Adopt a structured synthesis template that the coding tool can populate (theme, supporting quote count, contradicting evidence, recommended client action)
Pilot AI-assisted theme summarization on one study, with the senior researcher curating and rewriting rather than authoring from scratch
Maintain a versioned codebook with quarterly reviews so it does not silently rot as study types evolve

high.headline: Synthesis is a defensible practice asset
high.text: You have the systems most boutiques never get to. The use now is reducing senior hours per study without reducing rigor.
steps: Build a cross-study insights layer that surfaces patterns across past projects for repeat clients, this is a billable deliverable competitors cannot match
Train a junior researcher to run end-to-end synthesis using your codebook and templates, your senior time should be on interpretation and client narrative
Measure synthesis hours per study and target a 30% reduction over two quarters by tightening template usage and AI assistance

questions.text: How is the final report assembled?

answers.label: Built from scratch in slides every time
Template deck, heavily edited
Template deck with reusable section blocks
Modular template plus a content library of past slides and visuals
Structured report assembled from synthesis output with automated chart and quote insertion

questions.text: How many internal review rounds does a typical report go through before client delivery?

answers.label: 4+ rounds, scope often expands
3 rounds, frequent rework
2 rounds, mostly polish
1 review plus a final read
1 structured review with a clear sign-off checklist

questions.text: From last interview to client-ready report, how many calendar days?

answers.label: 15+ days
10 to 14 days
7 to 10 days
4 to 6 days
3 days or fewer

low.headline: Reports are eating your margin
low.text: Building reports from scratch every time is the single most visible source of margin compression in a boutique practice. Clients are paying you to think, not to format slides.
steps: Build a master report template with locked structure (objectives, method, key findings, theme detail, recommendations, appendix) and use it on every study
Create a slide library of your best visualizations, frameworks, and quote layouts tagged by study type so juniors can assemble 60% of a report in a day
Cap internal review at 2 structured rounds with a sign-off checklist, scope expansion in review is a leadership problem not a researcher problem

mid.headline: Reports are templated, assembly is still manual
mid.text: You have a template but the path from synthesis to a polished deck still consumes a senior person for days. This is where modular assembly and AI drafting pay off fastest.
steps: Move report assembly to a modular system where synthesis findings auto-populate a starter deck with placeholder charts and quote slots
Pilot AI-drafted executive summary and key findings narrative, with the senior researcher editing rather than authoring
Track report assembly hours per study and target a 40% reduction within one quarter, the room is there

high.headline: Delivery is fast, now compete on it
high.text: You can ship in under a week. Most of your competitors cannot. That speed is a sellable position, not just an operational nicety.
steps: Lead with delivery speed in your proposals and case studies, price a rapid-turnaround tier explicitly
Offer mid-study readouts as a paid deliverable, your assembly system makes the marginal cost low
Reinvest the saved senior hours into business development and thought leadership rather than absorbing them as more studies

cta.headline: Want the role-specific fix plan for your lowest category?
cta.description: Book a 30-minute strategy call. I'll walk you through your category scores, identify the single highest-impact fix for your role, and sketch what a 90-day implementation looks like for a practice your size. No pitch, no slides. If it is not a fit you leave with the plan anyway.
